overview.title: 📖 Overview: A Sandal's Nails and the Weight of a Tragic Memory
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 60a–60b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by settling the previous amud's ring contradiction with three different resolutions, then explains why an unperforated needle — seemingly just a hair tool, forbidden to use on Shabbat itself — may still be worn out. A new mishna then lists six items a man may not wear into the public domain: a spiked sandal, a single sandal without a wound to justify it, tefillin, an unauthenticated amulet, and war-gear — none of which carry sin-offering liability even if worn out. The Gemara devotes the rest of the daf to the spiked sandal, tracing its ban to a historic tragedy in a cave of refugees, and then works out exactly how many nails turn a sandal from a forbidden 'reinforced' shoe into a permitted, merely decorated one.

slides.title: 🔧 The Ring Contradiction, Resolved Three Ways
slides.subtitle: Does a sealed ring count by its ring, or by its seal?

lines.speaker: Mishna rule
lines.text: With a hook-board, follow its nails; with a ladder, follow its rungs; with a scale, follow its chains. The Rabbis: for all of these, everything follows the support (מַעֲמִיד).

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Then a ring should follow the ring itself, not the seal — so why does Rabbi Neḥemya treat a sealed ring differently for Shabbat, while the Kelim mishna calls a sealed ring an impure ornament just like a plain one?

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: No contradiction at all — the two mishnayot speak 'in respective terms': a sealed ring is a MAN's ornament, an unsealed ring is a WOMAN's ornament.

lines.speaker: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
lines.text: Don't compare impurity to Shabbat! Impurity follows the verse כְּלִי מַעֲשֶׂה ('an implement with which work is done') — a ring is that either way. Shabbat forbids only a burden: unsealed, it's a woman's ornament; sealed, it's a burden for her.

callout.label: Underlying idea:
callout.text: 'Everything follows the support' decides which PART defines a vessel's material for impurity — a separate question from whether a woman is likely to slip an item off and carry it on Shabbat.

slides.title: 📌 An Unperforated Needle — Why Permitted?
slides.subtitle: Three answers before the Gemara lands on one

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Yosef: a woman uses it to gather her hair and pin it to her hairnet
2️⃣ Abaye objects: then it's like a (impurity-)pure garter — permitted simply because modesty stops her from removing and showing it. Why did the mishna need to list it at all?
3️⃣ Rav Adda of Naresh answers instead: she uses it to part her hair
4️⃣ New problem: parting hair is itself forbidden on Shabbat — so what use does the needle serve ON Shabbat?

5️⃣ Rava: the needle has a gold plate on its other end. Weekdays, she parts her hair with it; Shabbat, she tucks it into her head-covering with the gold plate resting on her forehead — purely as an ornament

slides.title: 🥿 New Mishna: Six Things a Man May Not Wear Out
slides.subtitle: Forbidden ab initio — but none of them carry sin-offering liability
headers: Why it is forbidden ab initio
rows: Commemorates a tragedy that began on Shabbat — see next slide
Only forbidden when there is no wound on the foot to explain it
One might forget them and carry them through the public domain
An amulet not from a proven expert
It may not truly work, so it is just a burden, not a remedy
Armor, a helmet, and military boots (שִׁרְיוֹן, קַסְדָּא, מַגָּפַיִים)
War-gear, not an ornament fit for Shabbat

callout.label: Note:
callout.text: The mishna closes: 'and if he went out, he is not liable to bring a sin-offering' — every item here is only a rabbinic-level prohibition.

slides.title: ⚔️ The Cave Tragedy Behind the Spiked-Sandal Decree
slides.subtitle: Refugees from religious persecution, undone by the sound of nails

steps.content: 1️⃣ Shmuel: Jews fleeing religious persecution hid in a cave, agreeing — whoever wants to enter may enter, but no one may leave (a leaver risks revealing the hideout)

2️⃣ One man's sandal turned backward; his footprints looked like someone leaving. Fearing an enemy had spotted them, the group panicked, pushed one another, and killed more of their own than any enemy had
3️⃣ Rabbi Ilai ben Elazar's version: they merely heard the SOUND of a spiked sandal above the cave, and panicked the same way
4️⃣ Rami bar Yeḥezkel's version: it happened in a synagogue, hearing the sound from behind the building

5️⃣ In every version it happened on Shabbat — so the ban applies to Shabbat (and, since 'assemblage' applies equally, to Festivals too), but not to a fast day, a day of permitted labor unlike the original incident

slides.title: 🔨 Structural Nails vs. Decorative Nails
slides.subtitle: How many nails, and what kind, keep a sandal off the forbidden list

boxes.title: Forbidden — For Strength
items: Nails placed to reinforce the sole
Rabbi Yoḥanan: more than five per sandal
Rabbi Ḥanina: more than seven per sandal
Rav Ḥisda: four is the limit for a small sandal, five for a large one

boxes.title: Permitted — For Beauty
items: A small, decorative number of nails, arranged evenly on both sides and the strap
Sewn from inside: it becomes a 'shoe', not a 'sandal' — no decree at all (Rav Ashi)
Bent like tongs, or the whole sole covered in nails so the ground won't wear it down (Rav Sheshet)

boxes.title: Edge Cases
items: An uneven sole needs extra straightening nails — Rabbi Natan: up to seven; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: up to thirteen — not treated as a spiked sandal at all
If most nails fell out and only four or five remain, it is permitted

summary.principle: An item a person wears is judged both by its physical role — what part of it actually does the work — and by whether wearing it in public risks turning into carrying, whether through fear (a slave's seal), habit (an important woman's tiara), or simple forgetfulness; the spiked sandal shows how a single historic tragedy became a lasting, precisely calibrated Shabbat decree.

flowSteps.content: 🔧 Ring: impurity asks if it's a 'kli ma'aseh'; Shabbat asks only if it's a burden
🥿 New mishna: six items forbidden to wear out, none carrying sin-offering liability

columns.content: ⚔️ Spiked sandal banned to commemorate a Shabbat-cave tragedy of mistaken panic
🔨 Nails for strength = forbidden; a small decorative number = permitted

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: a rabbinic decree tied to a specific tragic incident is extended to comparable settings (Shabbat → Festival) but not to unrelated ones (a fast day)

quiz.q: How does Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak resolve the contradiction between the impurity-mishna and the Shabbat-mishna regarding a sealed ring?
o: He says the two mishnayot describe different rings entirely
He says ritual impurity and Shabbat use different criteria: impurity asks if it's 'an implement with which work is done' (true either way), Shabbat asks only if it's a burden (true only when sealed)
He says the dispute was never actually resolved
He says sealed rings cannot become impure
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak argues the two areas of halakha rest on entirely different verses and principles, so there is no real contradiction to begin with.

quiz.q: According to Rava, why may a woman go out on Shabbat with an unperforated needle, even though parting hair is forbidden that day?
o: Because it is disguised as a garter
Because it has a gold plate on its other end, which she rests against her forehead as an ornament on Shabbat instead of using it to part her hair
Because unperforated needles cannot become impure
Because the mishna never actually forbids it
quiz.e: Rava explains that on weekdays the needle parts her hair, but on Shabbat she wears it tucked into her head covering with its gold plate against her forehead, serving purely as an ornament.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what is the liability of a man who goes out on Shabbat wearing a spiked sandal or an unauthenticated amulet?
o: He is liable to bring a sin-offering
He is not liable to bring a sin-offering, even though it is forbidden ab initio
He is completely exempt, since there was never a prohibition
He is liable to receive lashes
quiz.e: The mishna closes its list with 'and if he went out, he is not liable to bring a sin-offering' — these are rabbinic-level prohibitions, not Torah-level carrying violations.

quiz.q: According to Shmuel, what triggered the incident that led the Sages to ban the spiked sandal?
o: A refugee's sandal turned backward, making his footprints look like someone leaving a hideout cave, which caused a panicked stampede
A sandal accidentally started a fire
A spiked sandal was stolen from the Temple
Soldiers used spiked sandals to break into a synagogue
quiz.e: Shmuel relates that Jews hiding from religious persecution in a cave panicked when one man's reversed sandal print looked like someone had left, leading them to trample one another.

quiz.q: What distinguishes nails placed in a sandal 'for strength' from nails placed 'for beauty'?
o: Beauty-nails are always gold, strength-nails are always iron
Strength-nails, inserted to reinforce the sole, are forbidden; a small decorative number of nails, arranged for appearance, is permitted
There is no halakhic difference between them
Strength-nails are only used on children's sandals
quiz.e: Rav Yehuda taught in Shmuel's name that nails for reinforcing the sandal's structure are forbidden, while a modest number placed for decoration (the sages debate the exact count) is permitted.
